label: Sloane MS 3188 — Mysteriorum Libri Quinque
fullRef: London, British Library, Sloane MS 3188. John Dee, 'Quinti Libri Mysteriorum' (spirit action diaries, 1581–1583).

dateRange.notes: Covers the earliest recorded angelic sessions, from December 1581 through spring 1583.

author: John Dee
description: Dee's diary of the earliest angelic sessions, recording conversations with the spirits Uriel, Michael, Raphael, and others as perceived through Kelley's scrying. Contains the Sigillum Dei Aemeth diagrams, the Holy Table specifications, and the first angelic communications.
contents: Spirit action records, December 1581 – spring 1583
Diagrams of the Sigillum Dei Aemeth
Specifications for the Holy Table and equipment
Early angelic communications and instructions
Records of multiple scryers before Kelley (Barnabas Saul, etc.)
notes: Well-preserved. In Dee's own hand. The manuscript's attribution and dating are not in dispute. Some folio ordering questions exist but do not affect content reliability.

label: Sloane MS 3189 — Liber Loagaeth
fullRef: London, British Library, Sloane MS 3189. John Dee, 'Liber Loagaeth' (Book of Speech from God), c. 1583–1584.

dateRange.notes: Dating based on contextual evidence from the action diaries; the manuscript itself is undated.

author: John Dee
description: The manuscript Dee identified as 'Liber Loagaeth' or 'The Book of Speech from God.' Contains 49 leaves of letter and number grids in patterns that have never been decoded. Dee understood this as the 'Book of Enoch' dictated in reverse order through Kelley's scrying.
contents: 49 leaves of letter/number grids
Title page identifying the work as 'Liber Loagaeth'
Grids of varying dimensions and structural complexity
No explanatory text or key within the manuscript itself
notes: The manuscript's existence and physical form are certain. Its content has never been decoded. Dee's identification of it as the 'Book of Enoch' is a primary-source claim about the material's nature, not an independent verification.

label: Sloane MS 3191 — Great Table and Related Material
fullRef: London, British Library, Sloane MS 3191. John Dee, tables, diagrams, and angelic material, c. 1583–1587.

dateRange.notes: Contains material from the mid-period through the Continental sessions. Includes the earliest surviving copy of the Great Table.

author: John Dee
description: Contains the Great Table of Earth in its earliest surviving form, along with related tabular and diagrammatic material from the Cracow and Prague sessions. This is the primary manuscript witness for the Great Table's original state.
contents: The Great Table (earliest surviving grid, 25×27)
Related angelic tables and hierarchies
Material from the Cracow sessions
Dee's notes on the Reformed Table (post-1587)
notes: Some individual cells in the Great Table are difficult to read due to ink fading and manuscript condition. The overall structure and most readings are clear. Scholarly disagreement exists on specific cell readings, particularly in areas of ink damage.

label: Cotton Appendix XLVI, Part I
fullRef: London, British Library, Cotton MS Appendix XLVI, Part I. John Dee, angelic action records, c. 1583–1587.
author: John Dee
description: Continuation of Dee's angelic action records, covering the later English sessions and the Continental period. This manuscript was the primary source for Casaubon's 1659 publication. It includes material not found in the Sloane manuscripts.
contents: Spirit action records, 1583–1587
Records of the Continental sessions (Cracow, Prague)
Material relating to the 19 Calls/Keys
Records leading up to the 1587 disruption
notes: This manuscript was the primary source Casaubon used for A True & Faithful Relation. Some scholars (notably Peterson) have identified places where Casaubon's transcription diverges from the manuscript.

label: Casaubon, A True & Faithful Relation (1659)
fullRef: Méric Casaubon, A True & Faithful Relation of What Passed for Many Yeers Between Dr. John Dee and Some Spirits (London, 1659).
description: The first published edition of Dee's spirit diaries. Casaubon presented the material as evidence of demonic deception, framing his publication as a cautionary tale. His editorial choices — what to include, exclude, and how to arrange the material — have shaped all subsequent reception of the Dee-Kelley sessions.
contents: Transcription of action records from Cotton Appendix XLVI
Casaubon's preface framing the material as demonic deception
Selected angelic communications and instructions
Some material from the Continental period
notes: Casaubon's transcription is generally faithful but not perfect. Peterson and others have identified divergences from the manuscript sources. Casaubon also made editorial selections — not all manuscript content appears in the printed edition. The uncertainty level reflects transcription accuracy, not the existence of the publication.

label: Golden Dawn — Rearranged Great Table
fullRef: S.L. MacGregor Mathers et al., Golden Dawn internal papers (c. 1888–1900). Arrangement of the Great Table with reassigned elemental quarters. Unpublished during the Order's active period; first published by Regardie (1937).

dateRange.notes: The exact date of Mathers' rearrangement is uncertain. The Golden Dawn was founded in 1888; the rearranged table was in use within the Order by the 1890s.

author: S.L. MacGregor Mathers
description: The Golden Dawn's rearrangement of Dee's Great Table, reassigning the elemental quarters (which element corresponds to which quadrant) and introducing the Tablet of Union as a central coordinating device. This rearrangement, not Dee's original, became the standard form used by most 20th- and 21st-century Enochian practitioners.
contents: Rearranged 25×27 Great Table grid
Reassigned elemental quarter correspondences
Tablet of Union (not present in Dee's original)
Hebrew letter correspondences added to the table
notes: The rearrangement is well-documented through Regardie's publication and surviving Golden Dawn papers. However, the exact reasoning behind Mathers' changes has never been fully explained in surviving documents. Some scholars suggest Mathers was working from a different manuscript source or a deliberate magical reinterpretation; others suggest he misread Dee's arrangement.

label: Regardie, The Golden Dawn (1937–1940)
fullRef: Israel Regardie, The Golden Dawn: An Account of the Teachings, Rites, and Ceremonies of the Order of the Golden Dawn, 4 vols. (Chicago: Aries Press, 1937–1940). Revised editions: 1971, 1984.

dateRange.notes: First edition published in four volumes, 1937–1940. Revised editions followed; the 1984 Llewellyn edition is most widely referenced.

author: Israel Regardie
description: Regardie's publication of the Golden Dawn's ritual papers, including their version of the Enochian system. For most modern practitioners, this book is the primary point of contact with Enochian material. It presents the Golden Dawn's rearranged Great Table, their system of Enochian correspondences, and their ritual framework.
contents: Golden Dawn's rearranged Great Table
Watchtower ritual framework
Enochian letter correspondences
Enochian pronunciation guide (Golden Dawn style)
Integration of Enochian material with the broader GD system
notes: The publication itself is well-documented and widely available. Regardie's editorial choices introduced some standardizations not present in the original GD papers. The 1984 revised edition corrected some typographical errors from earlier printings but also introduced new editorial decisions. When citing Regardie, the specific edition matters.

label: Crowley, The Vision and the Voice (1911/1952)
fullRef: Aleister Crowley, The Vision and the Voice, with Commentary and Other Papers (Liber 418). First partial publication in The Equinox I:5 (1911). Full publication with commentary: Sangreal Foundation, 1972; revised critical edition in The Equinox IV:2 (Samuel Weiser, 1998).

dateRange.notes: The scrying sessions took place in the Algerian desert in November–December 1909. First partial publication in The Equinox, 1911. Full publication with commentary much later.

author: Aleister Crowley
description: Crowley's record of his scrying of the 30 Aethyrs, conducted in the North African desert in 1909 with Victor Neuburg as assistant. This is the most significant experiential account of the Aethyrs since Dee and Kelley, and the only one that attempts all 30 in sequence. Crowley's account is deeply personal, heavily influenced by his Thelemic framework, and unlike anything in Dee's original records.
contents: Records of scrying all 30 Aethyrs
Commentary written decades later (1920s–1940s)
Thelemic interpretive framework applied to Enochian material
Account of the crossing of the Abyss (ZAX, the 10th Aethyr)
notes: The publication history is complex. The 1911 Equinox publication is partial. The commentary was written much later. Different editions contain different material. The experiential claims are Crowley's own and cannot be independently verified. As a primary source for Crowley's experience, the text is reliable; as evidence about the Aethyrs themselves, it carries an ○ badge.

label: Laycock, The Complete Enochian Dictionary (1978/1994)
fullRef: Donald C. Laycock, The Complete Enochian Dictionary: A Dictionary of the Angelic Language as Revealed to Dr. John Dee and Edward Kelley (London: Askin Publishers, 1978; revised edition: York Beach, ME: Samuel Weiser, 1994).

dateRange.notes: First edition 1978. Revised and expanded edition 1994.

author: Donald C. Laycock
description: The most systematic linguistic analysis of the Enochian language. Laycock, a professional linguist, compiled a comprehensive dictionary from the Calls and other Enochian texts, analyzed the language's phonological and grammatical properties, and assessed whether it exhibits the features of a natural language, a constructed language, or a glossolalic production.
contents: Complete Enochian-English dictionary
Phonological analysis of Enochian
Grammatical analysis of Enochian syntax
Assessment of the language's linguistic status
Transcription notes for Liber Loagaeth (partial)
notes: Laycock's dictionary is the scholarly standard for Enochian lexicography. His linguistic analysis remains the most thorough available. Some of his specific conclusions (particularly regarding whether the language is 'genuine') have been debated by subsequent scholars, but his data compilation is universally respected.

label: Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels (1999)
fullRef: Deborah E. Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999).
author: Deborah E. Harkness
description: A landmark academic study of Dee's angelic conversations, placing them within the context of Elizabethan natural philosophy, Cabala, and apocalyptic expectation. Harkness argues that Dee's angel magic was not a departure from his scientific work but an extension of it — an attempt to access divine knowledge through angelic intermediaries.
contents: Contextual analysis of Dee's angel magic within Elizabethan natural philosophy
Detailed examination of the angelic session records
Analysis of Dee's Cabalistic and alchemical frameworks
Discussion of Dee's apocalyptic expectations and their role in the sessions
notes: Published by Cambridge University Press. Widely cited in subsequent Dee scholarship. Harkness's interpretive framework (angel magic as natural philosophy) has been influential but is not the only scholarly reading. Szönyi (2004) and Clucas (2006) offer complementary and occasionally contrasting perspectives.

label: Woolley, The Queen's Conjurer (2001)
fullRef: Benjamin Woolley, The Queen's Conjurer: The Science and Magic of Dr. John Dee, Adviser to Queen Elizabeth I (New York: Henry Holt, 2001).
author: Benjamin Woolley
description: A biographical study of Dee that integrates the angel sessions into the broader narrative of his life and career. More accessible than Harkness (1999) and written for a general audience, but grounded in primary source research. Woolley gives significant attention to Kelley's role and the psychological dynamics of the partnership.
contents: Full biography of Dee from birth to death
Account of the Dee-Kelley partnership
Discussion of Kelley's background and motivations
Narrative of the Continental journey and its aftermath
notes: Written for a general audience, not an academic monograph. Some scholars consider Woolley's treatment of Kelley more sympathetic and psychologically nuanced than other accounts. Woolley does not resolve the sincerity-vs-fabrication question but presents it with care.

label: Peterson, John Dee's Five Books of Mystery (2003)
fullRef: Joseph H. Peterson, ed., John Dee's Five Books of Mystery: Original Sourcebook of Enochian Magic (York Beach, ME: Red Wheel/Weiser, 2003).
description: A modern critical edition of Sloane MS 3188 (Mysteriorum Libri Quinque). Peterson's transcription is the most accessible and carefully edited modern version of the earliest angelic session records. His editorial apparatus identifies differences between the manuscript and Casaubon's 1659 printed edition.
contents: Complete transcription of Sloane MS 3188
Editorial apparatus comparing manuscript to Casaubon 1659
Diagrams and tables reproduced from the manuscript
Introduction contextualizing the material
notes: Peterson's transcription is widely regarded as the most reliable modern edition of Sloane 3188. His digital editions (esotericarchives.com) are also valuable but should be checked against the print edition where possible, as the digital versions have been updated over time.

label: Peterson — Liber Loagaeth Transcription (Digital)
fullRef: Joseph H. Peterson, transcription of Sloane MS 3189, available at esotericarchives.com (ongoing, various dates).

dateRange.notes: Peterson's digital transcription work has been ongoing. Specific dates for individual leaf transcriptions are not always documented.

description: Peterson's partial digital transcription of Liber Loagaeth (Sloane MS 3189). Covers a subset of the 49 leaves. This is one of the few publicly available transcriptions of the manuscript and is used as a reference point by subsequent researchers.
contents: Partial transcription of Liber Loagaeth leaves
Structural notes on grid dimensions and layout
Cross-references to other Dee manuscripts
notes: The transcription is valuable but incomplete. Digital transcriptions may have been updated over time without version tracking. Individual cell readings should be verified against the manuscript where possible. The uncertainty level reflects the transcription's completeness and the inherent difficulty of reading the manuscript, not any doubt about Peterson's competence.

label: Szönyi, John Dee's Occultism (2004)
fullRef: György E. Szönyi, John Dee's Occultism: Magical Exaltation through Powerful Signs (Albany: SUNY Press, 2004).
author: György E. Szönyi
description: An academic study situating Dee's occult practices within Renaissance semiotic theory. Szönyi argues that Dee's angel magic was fundamentally an exercise in sign manipulation — an attempt to access the divine through 'powerful signs' that could bridge the human and angelic realms. This reading complements Harkness's natural-philosophy interpretation.
contents: Semiotic analysis of Dee's magical practices
Discussion of the Enochian system as a sign system
Comparative analysis with other Renaissance magi
Theoretical framework connecting magic and semiotics
notes: Published by SUNY Press. An academic monograph with a theoretical rather than biographical focus. Szönyi's semiotic framework is distinctive and not universally adopted, but his scholarship is rigorous and widely cited.

label: Leitch, The Angelical Language, Vol. I (2009)
fullRef: Aaron Leitch, The Angelical Language, Volume I: The Complete History and Mythos of the Tongue of Angels (Woodbury, MN: Llewellyn, 2010).
author: Aaron Leitch
description: A practitioner-scholar's study of the Enochian language, combining historical research with practical magical perspective. Leitch draws on primary manuscript sources and modern scholarship while maintaining an operational magical framework. His work on Liber Loagaeth includes structural analysis of selected leaves.
contents: History of the Enochian language's transmission
Analysis of the language's phonology and structure
Discussion of Liber Loagaeth's grid structures
Comparison with other angelic and divine languages in Western esotericism
notes: Leitch occupies an intermediate position between academic scholarship and practitioner tradition. His historical research is generally sound and well-sourced, but his interpretive framework is informed by active magical practice. The Archive treats his factual claims at ◇ when independently verifiable, and ○ when grounded in practitioner experience.
